descriptive.n: Used before a noun, this adjective means giving details about what something is like, so a descriptive paragraph paints a picture in words. It also has a technical sense in grammar and science: descriptive statistics summarise data, while descriptive grammar records how people really speak. Stress falls on the second syllable: de-SCRIP-tive. It is often paired with the opposite idea, prescriptive, which tells people what they should do. Typical partners are descriptive title, descriptive name and descriptive writing. In casual speech people just say that a word or phrase is vivid.
x: Her descriptive essay about the market made every reader hungry.
Choose a descriptive file name so you can find the document later.
Descriptive statistics, such as the average, summarise a data set without predicting anything.

disappointment.n: Both a feeling and a thing can be a disappointment. You feel disappointment when hopes are not met, and a person, event or product can be a disappointment if it falls short. Stress is on the third syllable: dis-ap-POINT-ment. Common patterns are disappointment at or about an event, disappointment in a person, and to the disappointment of someone. Typical collocations include bitter, deep and sense of disappointment. It is neutral in register and fits both daily talk and formal letters. A milder everyday alternative is letdown.
x: To her great disappointment, the concert was cancelled at the last minute.
The final season was a real disappointment after such a strong start.
He tried to hide his disappointment when he heard he had not been chosen.

dive.n: As a verb it covers a head-first jump into water, swimming underwater with equipment, and any sudden downward movement, from birds to share prices. Regular in British English (dived) and often dove in American English, while the past participle is dived in both. Typical patterns are dive into the pool, dive for cover and dive into a topic, which means start something with enthusiasm. A dive in prices is a sharp fall. Do not mix it up with dip, which is smaller and gentler. In casual speech, jump in can replace the figurative sense.
x: The children dive from the wooden pier every summer afternoon.
When the alarm sounded, everyone had to dive under their desks.
Let us dive straight into the main problem and skip the introductions.

dull.n: This adjective has three common uses: boring (a dull lecture), not bright or shiny (a dull colour, a dull sky), and not sharp (a dull knife or a dull pain). It is one syllable and rhymes with gull. Used about a person, it can sound rude, so describe the situation instead. The opposite changes with the meaning: exciting, bright or sharp. Typical partners are dull routine, dull weather and dull ache. A common idiom is all work and no play makes Jack a dull boy. In casual talk, boring is the plainest synonym.
x: The sky stayed dull and grey all through the weekend.
I need a new knife because this one has gone dull.
He felt a dull ache in his shoulder after carrying the heavy bags.

engagement.n: Several meanings share this noun, and context decides which is meant. It can be a promise to marry, a prior appointment (a speaking engagement), involvement or interest (customer engagement, a key business metric), or a military battle. Stress is on the second syllable: en-GAGE-ment. Typical collocations are engagement ring, previous engagement and engagement rate. Saying you have a prior engagement is a polite, slightly formal way to decline an invitation. In plain speech, use appointment or plans for the schedule sense. Related verbs include engage and get engaged.
x: Their engagement was announced at the family dinner on Sunday.
Sorry, I cannot come because of a prior engagement that evening.
Short videos usually bring higher engagement than long written posts.

fabric.n: A general word for woven or knitted material used for clothes, curtains and furniture. It is usually uncountable (a lot of fabric), though a countable use appears when comparing types (cotton and wool fabrics). Stress falls on the first syllable: FAB-ric. A second, figurative sense is the basic structure of a society or system, as in the fabric of society. Common collocations are soft fabric, waterproof fabric and fabric softener. Cloth is nearly equal in daily use, while material is the most general everyday word. Fabric shops sell it by the metre.
x: She chose a light linen fabric for the summer curtains.
Wash this fabric in cold water so the colours do not fade.
Strong neighbourhood ties are part of the social fabric of a small town.

graphics.n: Treated as a plural-form noun that usually takes a singular verb when it names a field or feature (the graphics are impressive is also correct for visual elements). It refers to images, charts and designs, especially on a screen, and also to the quality of visuals in video games. Stress is on the first syllable: GRAPH-ics. Typical collocations are computer graphics, graphics card, motion graphics and graphic design. Do not confuse it with graphic as an adjective, meaning vivid or shockingly detailed. In everyday language, visuals or pictures can stand in.
x: The game has amazing graphics, but it runs slowly on old laptops.
Our designer added bright graphics to make the report easier to read.
She studies computer graphics at university and wants to work on films.

humidity.n: An uncountable noun for the amount of water vapour in the air, usually given as a percentage. Stress is on the second syllable: hyoo-MID-i-ty. People often talk about relative humidity in weather reports, and a hygrometer measures it. Common partners are high humidity, low humidity and humidity level. The related adjective is humid, which suggests heavy, sticky air and is used for climates, not for objects. In casual talk, people simply say it is muggy or damp, though damp refers to things being slightly wet, not to the air in general.
x: Humidity in the rainforest stays above ninety percent all year.
A small device on the wall shows the temperature and humidity of the room.
Wood furniture can crack if the humidity drops too low in winter.

individually.n: An adverb meaning one by one or separately, rather than as a group. It often follows a verb (treated individually) or comes before a participle (individually packed). Stress falls on the third syllable: in-di-VID-yoo-a-lee. It contrasts with collectively and together. Typical collocations are individually wrapped, individually priced and speak to each person individually. In formal writing it is common in contracts and product descriptions. Casual alternatives include separately and one at a time. Do not confuse it with personally, which stresses that you yourself do something.
x: The teacher spoke to each student individually after the exam.
These cookies are sold individually or in boxes of twelve.
Individually, the problems look small, but together they cost us a lot.

inference.n: A formal noun for a conclusion reached by reasoning from evidence, rather than from direct statement. Stress is on the first syllable: IN-fer-ence. Typical patterns are make an inference, draw an inference and by inference. It is common in reading tests, science and logic. Do not confuse it with imply: a writer implies, while a reader infers. The verb is infer, and the adjective inferential is rare. Related words are conclusion and deduction, though deduction suggests a stricter logical step. In casual speech, people say they worked something out or guessed from clues.
x: From the empty desks, we drew the inference that the meeting had finished.
Good readers make inferences about a character's feelings from small details.
That is only an inference, so please do not present it as a fact.

intently.n: An adverb meaning with close, fixed attention. It usually follows verbs of perceiving or thinking, such as listen, watch, stare and study, and it suggests concentration rather than mere looking. Stress is on the second syllable: in-TENT-ly. It sounds a little literary and works well in storytelling and descriptions of behaviour. The adjective intent means determined, as in intent on winning. A common alternative in speech is closely or carefully. Do not use it for general effort, since it describes attention, not hard work.
x: The cat watched the bird intently without moving a single muscle.
She listened intently as the doctor explained the results.
He studied the map intently before choosing the left path.

irrelevant.n: An adjective for something that has no useful connection to the matter being discussed. The pattern is irrelevant to something, and it often appears in meetings, exams and legal talk, as in irrelevant evidence or irrelevant details. Stress falls on the second syllable: i-REL-e-vant, and the opposite is relevant. It can sound blunt when used about a person's comment, so many speakers soften it with a bit off topic. Typical intensifiers are largely, entirely and completely irrelevant. Related nouns are irrelevance and irrelevancy.
x: His age is irrelevant to whether he can do the job well.
The judge told the jury to ignore irrelevant evidence.
Most of the questions were irrelevant, so the interview felt like a waste of time.

machinery.n: An uncountable noun for machines considered together, or for the working parts of a machine. It takes a singular verb and has no plural or article with a number, so say a piece of machinery, not a machinery. Stress is on the second syllable: ma-SHEEN-er-y, with the ch sounded as sh. A figurative use is the machinery of government. Typical collocations are heavy machinery, farm machinery and agricultural machinery. Equipment is broader and covers tools, while machine is the countable form. In everyday talk, people say the machines.
x: Workers must wear ear protection near the noisy machinery.
Farm machinery has become much more expensive over the last decade.
The machinery of local government can be slow to respond to small complaints.

neat.n: A short, everyday adjective that mostly means tidy and carefully arranged, as in neat handwriting or a neat desk. In American English it is also a casual way to say great or clever (a neat trick), and in British English it describes a drink served without ice or mixers, as in whisky neat. Do not confuse the sound with net. Common partners are neat and tidy, neat row and neatly dressed. The adverb is neatly. Alternatives are tidy, orderly or, for the casual sense, cool.
x: Her notes were so neat that everyone borrowed them before exams.
The books on the shelf stood in a neat row, sorted by size.
That is a neat idea, and it saves us a whole afternoon of work.

prestigious.n: An adjective meaning highly respected and admired, so it brings status to whoever belongs to or wins it. It describes institutions, awards, jobs and addresses: a prestigious university, prize or firm. Stress is on the second syllable: pre-STEEJ-us, and the noun is prestige. It is positive and formal, common in news and application letters. Do not use it for people directly; say respected or distinguished instead. A casual alternative is top, or well known. Collocations include prestigious award, prestigious post and highly prestigious.
x: She won a prestigious scholarship to study music in Vienna.
Working at such a prestigious firm will look excellent on your resume.
The prize is one of the most prestigious in the field of architecture.

preview.n: As a noun, it means a chance to see or hear part of something before the general public, such as a film preview, or a short sample of what comes later. As a verb, it means to look at something in advance, and software uses it for a window showing a file before opening. Stress falls on the first syllable of the noun: PREE-view. Common patterns are a preview of and sneak preview. Related words include trailer for films and teaser for adverts. In casual speech, people say a first look.
x: The studio held a special preview of the film for the critics.
Click the small icon to preview the document before you print it.
This paragraph gives a short preview of what the next chapter covers.

prospective.n: An adjective that goes before a noun and means likely to be or to happen in the future. It describes people in a role they may soon hold: a prospective buyer, tenant, student or employer. Stress falls on the second syllable: pro-SPEC-tive. It is formal and common in business and property writing. Do not confuse it with perspective, which means a point of view. It cannot follow a linking verb, so do not say the buyer is prospective. A plainer alternative is potential, which has a slightly weaker, more speculative sense.
x: The agent showed the flat to several prospective tenants on Saturday.
Prospective students can visit the campus during the open day.
He is writing a letter to a prospective employer in Toronto.

rebate.n: A noun for an amount of money paid back to you after you have already paid in full, often by a manufacturer or a tax office. It is different from a discount, which lowers the price at the moment of purchase. Stress is on the first syllable in the noun: REE-bate, but the verb is usually re-BATE. Typical collocations are tax rebate, energy rebate, claim a rebate and mail-in rebate. It is common in shopping and finance texts. A casual alternative is money back, or refund when the full amount comes back.
x: You can claim a rebate if you buy an energy-saving fridge.
The tax office sent him a rebate of two hundred dollars.
Remember to mail the form, or you will not get your rebate.

recipient.n: A formal noun for a person or organisation that receives something, such as a letter, a payment, a gift, an award or an organ. Stress falls on the second syllable: re-SIP-i-ent. It is used in business, law, medicine and email contexts, and it pairs with sender or donor. Typical collocations are the intended recipient, award recipient, recipient of aid and email recipient. Do not confuse it with receptionist. In casual speech, the person receiving it or simply the receiver works well, though receiver sounds odd for gifts.
x: Please check the address so the parcel reaches the correct recipient.
She was the youngest recipient of the national prize for science.
Add the recipient's name before you press the send button.

redesign.n: A verb meaning to change the design of something, from a logo or website to a whole building or process. It can also be a noun, as in a complete redesign. Stress in the verb is on the second syllable: ree-di-ZINE, but the noun often stresses the first: REE-di-zine. The prefix re- shows that a design already existed, so do not use it for first-time creation. It takes a direct object and is often used with companies and teams. Common collocations are redesign the layout, a total redesign and a major redesign. Casual alternatives are rework and revamp.
x: The airline plans to redesign its seats to give passengers more legroom.
After the redesign, our app is much easier to navigate.
They had to redesign the kitchen because the old layout wasted space.

retrieve.n: A formal verb meaning to get something back, often from a place where it was stored or lost, as with data from a computer, a bag from storage or a ball from the water. Stress falls on the second syllable: re-TREEV. Typical patterns are retrieve something from somewhere, retrieve information and retrieve a password. The noun is retrieval, and a retriever is a dog that fetches things. In plain speech, fetch, get back or recover are common, with recover suggesting something lost or damaged. It is neutral to formal and common in IT.
x: The software can retrieve deleted photos from the memory card.
He went back to the car to retrieve his umbrella.
Divers managed to retrieve the box from the bottom of the lake.

seldom.n: An adverb meaning not often, and a more formal or literary partner of rarely. It normally sits before the main verb (she seldom complains), after be (he is seldom late), and can start a sentence with inversion for emphasis: Seldom have I seen such talent. It already has a negative meaning, so do not add not or never. The common pattern seldom or never is a set phrase. Stress is on the first syllable: SEL-dom. In everyday conversation, rarely and not often are more usual.
x: My grandfather seldom uses a computer, but he loves his old radio.
Seldom have I heard such a clear and honest explanation.
It rains here seldom, so the farmers depend on wells.

skim.n: A verb with two meanings. The reading sense is to look quickly through a text to get the main idea, usually without reading every word, and it goes well with through or over. The physical sense is to move lightly across a surface, as when a stone skims the water, or to remove something floating, such as skimming fat from soup. It is regular: skimmed, skimming. Skim reading differs from scanning, which looks for one particular detail. Casual alternatives are glance through and flick through.
x: I only had time to skim the email before the call began.
Swallows skim over the lake to catch insects in the evening.
Skim the headings first, and then read the sections that matter most.

spouse.n: A formal, gender-neutral noun for a husband or wife. It appears on forms, in legal documents and in company policies, where writers want to include same-sex marriages without naming gender. It rhymes with house and is pronounced as one syllable. In conversation, people usually say my husband, my wife or my partner instead, because spouse can sound stiff. Typical collocations are spouse and children, current spouse and surviving spouse. Do not confuse it with spouse as a verb, which does not exist in English.
x: Please write your spouse's name in the emergency contact section.
Both spouses must sign the document before the bank will approve the loan.
Many employers offer health cover for employees and their spouses.

subsidize.n: A verb meaning to pay part of the cost of something so that it is cheaper for others. Governments subsidize farming, housing and public transport, and companies may subsidize canteens. American spelling uses a z; British writers often prefer subsidise. Stress is on the first syllable: SUB-si-dize. The noun is subsidy, and the adjective is subsidised. It is formal and used in economics and politics. A casual alternative is help pay for. Be careful: subsidize implies ongoing support, not a single gift or a loan.
x: The city will subsidize bus tickets for students and retired people.
Critics say governments should not subsidize fossil fuels any longer.
Our firm helps to subsidize language courses for all its staff.

tactic.n: A noun for a specific action or plan used to reach a goal, usually part of a larger strategy. It is most often used in the plural, tactics, in sports, business and politics: delay tactics, scare tactics and negotiating tactics. Stress is on the first syllable: TAK-tik. Do not confuse it with strategy, which is the overall long-term plan, while tactics are the smaller steps. The adjective tactical often appears in military and sports contexts, and a person who is tactful is polite, which is a different word. A plain alternative is method or approach.
x: Their main tactic was to keep the ball and wait for a mistake.
Some shops use scare tactics to make customers buy extra insurance.
If this tactic fails, we will try a different approach next week.

terrific.n: An informal adjective meaning excellent or very good, widely used in American English to praise people, ideas and results. Stress is on the second syllable: te-RIF-ik. Its older meaning, causing terror, is rare today, and it is nearly the same word as terrifying, so context is important. It may also mean extreme, as in a terrific noise. It is common in spoken praise: That is terrific news! It sounds a little old-fashioned to younger British speakers, who might say brilliant or great.
x: That is terrific news, and I am so glad you told me.
The new manager has done a terrific job with the team.
We had a terrific time at the beach, and the weather was perfect.

vacancy.n: A noun used for a job that nobody is doing and is open to applicants, and also for a room or flat that is free to rent. Stress falls on the first syllable: VAY-kan-see. Typical patterns are fill a vacancy, a vacancy for a chef, and no vacancies on hotel signs. It is countable in the job sense and uncountable in the vacancy-rate sense. The adjective is vacant, as in a vacant seat. Do not confuse it with position, which is the job itself, not the opening. In casual talk, people say an opening.
x: The school has a vacancy for a part-time science teacher.
We drove past three motels, but each one showed a no vacancy sign.
It took the company six months to fill the vacancy in accounting.

wrinkle.n: A small line or fold in skin or fabric. As a noun it also means a small problem or unexpected difficulty, as in an unexpected wrinkle in the plan. As a verb, it describes making or getting such folds, and the participle wrinkled is common: a wrinkled shirt. Stress is on the first syllable: RING-kul, with the w silent. Typical collocations are iron out the wrinkles, wrinkle-free fabric and wrinkles around the eyes. Casual alternatives for cloth are crease and crumple.
x: There was a wrinkle in our plans when the venue raised its price.
This shirt is wrinkle-free, so you will not need to iron it.
He had deep wrinkles around his eyes from years of smiling.

announcer.n: A person whose job is to read out information to an audience, for example on radio, television, at a station or at a sporting event. The word comes from announce, and its stress falls on the second syllable: a-NOUN-ser. Typical collocations are radio announcer, station announcer, sports announcer and public address announcer. It is not the same as presenter or host, who usually run a whole show and speak freely, while an announcer mostly delivers short, planned messages. In casual talk, people simply refer to the voice over the speaker.
x: The announcer told passengers that platform four had changed.
He worked as a radio announcer before becoming a news reporter.
The stadium announcer read the team lists to the cheering crowd.

appetizer.n: The American word for a small dish served before the main course, which British speakers more often call a starter. The stress falls on the first syllable: AP-i-ty-zer. Restaurants list it on the menu under starters or appetizers, and a platter of small bites for sharing is a typical example. Typical patterns are order an appetizer, share an appetizer and as an appetizer. Do not confuse it with dessert, which comes after. The spelling appetiser is British. In casual speech, people say they will have a little something to start.
x: We shared a plate of fried calamari as an appetizer.
The waiter asked if we wanted an appetizer before the main dish.
Soup is the cheapest appetizer on the menu, and it tastes wonderful.

booklet.n: A small, thin book, usually with a paper cover, that gives information, instructions or a program. It is a countable noun, often used for brochures, manuals and exhibition guides. Stress is on the first syllable: BOOK-let. The ending -let means small, as in leaflet and piglet, which helps explain the word. A booklet is longer and more bound than a leaflet, which is a single sheet. Common collocations are an instruction booklet, a free booklet and a safety booklet. In casual speech, people might say a little guide.
x: A free booklet about local walks is available at the tourist office.
Read the instruction booklet before you assemble the shelves.
The museum gave every visitor a booklet with maps and short histories.

briefcase.n: A flat, rectangular case, usually leather or hard plastic, used for carrying papers, a laptop and small business items. It has a handle and often a lock. It is a compound noun written as one word, with stress on the first part: BREEF-kayss. It suggests formal office work, so it can sound a bit old-fashioned today, when many people use a laptop bag or backpack. Typical collocations are carry a briefcase, open the briefcase and leather briefcase. Do not confuse it with suitcase, which is for clothes on trips.
x: She put the contract in her briefcase and hurried to the station.
His old leather briefcase was a gift from his father.
The security guard asked him to open his briefcase at the entrance.

businessperson.n: A gender-neutral noun for someone who works in business, especially a person who owns, runs or invests in a company. It is written as one word, with stress on the first syllable: BIZ-nis-per-sun. The plural is businesspeople, not businesspersons. It replaces the older businessman and businesswoman when the gender does not matter or is unknown. Typical collocations are successful businessperson, local businessperson and international businesspeople. Entrepreneur is a close word but suggests starting new ventures. In casual speech, people often say they work in business.
x: A young businessperson from Lagos spoke at the trade fair.
Every businessperson on the team travels abroad several times a year.
As a busy businessperson, she rarely has time for long lunches.

caller.n: A person making a phone call, seen from the side of the one receiving it, and also someone who phones a radio program. It is a countable noun, and stress falls on the first syllable: KAW-ler. Typical collocations are the caller ID, an anonymous caller, regular caller and a hoax caller. In older British English, a caller can also be a visitor who stops by, which is now rare. Do not confuse it with receiver, who gets the call. In casual speech, people often say who is calling instead of asking for the caller.
x: The caller refused to give his name and hung up quickly.
Our receptionist asks every caller to spell their surname.
Three callers to the radio show disagreed with the host.

cordless.n: An adjective meaning working without an electric cord, and it is used for phones, drills, kettles and other tools powered by a battery or a base station. Stress falls on the first syllable: KORD-less, and the suffix -less means without, as in wireless. It usually appears before a noun. Typical collocations are a cordless phone, cordless drill and cordless vacuum cleaner. It is often paired with rechargeable. Cordless is slightly different from wireless, which describes radio links such as Wi-Fi, not a power supply. Casual speech sometimes drops the word and says handheld.
x: He fixed the shelf quickly with a cordless drill.
A cordless vacuum cleaner makes it easier to clean the stairs.
I took the cordless phone into the garden to finish the call.

cushion.n: A soft bag filled with foam, feathers or similar material, placed on a chair, sofa or floor for comfort or decoration. It is also a verb meaning to soften a blow or a bad effect: savings can cushion a fall in income. In American English, it is a close partner to pillow, but a pillow is for the head. Stress is on the first syllable: KOOSH-un. Typical collocations are sofa cushion, seat cushion and cushion cover. A cushion against something is a financial buffer or protection.
x: She put a cushion behind her back and opened the book.
A thick layer of snow helped to cushion the child's fall.
Savings can cushion the effect of losing a job for a few months.

diamond.n: A very hard, clear gem made of carbon, valued in jewellery and also used on industrial cutting tools. The word has three letters in the middle that are often misspoken: the usual pronunciation has two syllables, DY-mund, though some people say three. It also means a shape with four equal sides tilted upright, a playing card suit and the field in baseball. Typical collocations are diamond ring, diamond mine, rough diamond and diamond anniversary, which marks sixty years. A plain alternative for the shape is rhombus.
x: He asked her to marry him with a diamond ring on a quiet beach.
The old mine once produced the largest diamond in the region.
The children drew a red diamond in the middle of the flag.

doorman.n: A man whose job is to stand at the entrance of a hotel, apartment block or club to welcome people, open the door and call taxis. It is a compound noun with stress on the first syllable: DOR-man. The plural is doormen. In American English, it is especially connected with apartment buildings in New York. Because it names a man, some employers use the neutral term door attendant. In British English, a similar job at a nightclub is called a bouncer, who checks guests and removes troublemakers.
x: The doorman held an umbrella over us as we left the taxi.
Please leave the package with the doorman if I am not at home.
Our building has a friendly doorman who knows every tenant by name.

explorer.n: A person who travels through unknown or little-known places to learn about them, such as a polar or ocean explorer. It is a countable noun, and the stress falls on the second syllable: ik-SPLOR-er. The verb is explore, and the noun exploration refers to the activity. By extension, it can mean anyone curious about a new subject, as in a young explorer of science. Typical collocations are polar explorer, famous explorer and early explorers. Do not confuse it with adventurer, who seeks excitement more than knowledge. Casual speech may say traveller.
x: The explorer spent two years mapping rivers in the Amazon.
Early explorers often depended on local guides for food and directions.
Our toddler is a little explorer who opens every cupboard in the house.

extinguisher.n: A portable metal container that sprays water, foam or powder to put out a small fire, almost always in the phrase fire extinguisher. It comes from the verb extinguish, meaning to put out. Stress is on the second syllable: ik-STING-gwi-sher. Offices and public buildings must keep one near exits, and staff should know how to use it. The typical collocations are fire extinguisher, extinguisher training and portable extinguisher. Do not confuse it with a sprinkler, which is fixed to the ceiling and works automatically. In casual talk, people simply say fire thing, rarely.
x: The cook grabbed the extinguisher and put out the flames in seconds.
Each extinguisher is checked once a year by a qualified technician.
Please do not move the extinguisher from its place beside the stairs.

gasoline.n: The American word for the liquid fuel that powers most cars, usually shortened to gas in everyday speech. British speakers say petrol, so be careful with the word gas, which also means a natural gas for heating. Stress falls on the first syllable: GAS-uh-leen. It is uncountable, so say some gasoline, not a gasoline. Typical collocations are unleaded gasoline, gasoline prices, gasoline engine and run out of gasoline. It is flammable and should be handled with care. Diesel is a different fuel used in other engines.
x: We stopped at a station to fill the tank with gasoline.
Rising gasoline costs made many families buy smaller cars.
Never store gasoline in a plastic bottle inside the house.

hiker.n: A person who goes for a long walk in the countryside or mountains for pleasure, usually along marked paths. The verb is hike, and in American English it is the main word, while British speakers often say walker or rambler. Stress falls on the first syllable: HY-ker. Typical collocations are experienced hiker, hiker's trail and lost hiker. Hikers carry boots, water and maps. Do not confuse it with backpacker, who travels with a bag across countries, or climber, who needs ropes. A quick alternative in casual talk is simply walker.
x: The hiker followed the trail along the river until sunset.
Rescue teams found the missing hiker safe in a small cabin.
Experienced hikers always check the weather before they leave.

hotline.n: A phone line that gives direct, quick access to advice or help, often open at all times, such as a crisis hotline or a customer service hotline. It is a compound noun with stress on the first part: HOT-line. The related use in politics means a direct communication link between leaders. Typical collocations are call the hotline, hotline number, 24-hour hotline and help hotline. In casual speech, people say helpline in British English, which is almost equal. Do not confuse it with a hot line, two words, which would mean an actual warm wire.
x: Call the hotline if you notice anything suspicious in the building.
The bank set up a hotline for customers who lost their cards.
Volunteers answer the hotline day and night throughout the winter.

housekeeper.n: A person employed to clean and look after a house, hotel or other building, and sometimes to manage the household, cook and run errands. It is a compound noun with stress on the first part: HOUS-kee-per. In hotels, the head of the cleaning staff is the head housekeeper, and the department is called housekeeping. It differs from housewife, a woman who is not paid. Do not confuse it with house-sitter. In casual speech, people say cleaner for a short, simple job, and a maid is a more old-fashioned term.
x: The housekeeper changes the sheets and towels in every room.
They hired a housekeeper to look after the large country house.
Please tell the housekeeper if you need extra pillows tonight.

hurricane.n: A violent storm with very strong winds and heavy rain that forms over warm ocean water, mainly in the Atlantic and northeastern Pacific. The same kind of storm is a typhoon in the western Pacific and a cyclone in the Indian Ocean. Stress falls on the first syllable: HUR-i-kane. Typical collocations are hurricane season, hurricane warning, category five hurricane and hurricane damage. Forecasters give hurricanes personal names. In casual talk, people also use the word figuratively for a chaotic force, as in a hurricane of emails.
x: Thousands of residents left the coast before the hurricane arrived.
Hurricane season in the Caribbean runs from June to November.
A hurricane of angry messages hit our inbox after the announcement.

jewelry.n: An uncountable noun for decorative items such as rings, necklaces, bracelets and earrings, usually worn on the body. It is spelled jewelry in American English and jewellery in British English. Because it is uncountable, you say a piece of jewelry, not a jewelry. Stress falls on the first syllable: JOO-ul-ree. Typical collocations are gold jewelry, costume jewelry, jewelry box and jewelry store. Costume jewelry means cheap, fashion pieces without precious stones. A plain alternative is accessories, which can also include bags and belts.
x: She keeps her grandmother's jewelry in a small wooden box.
Please remove all jewelry before passing through the metal detector.
The shop sells handmade silver jewelry from local artists.

mower.n: A machine that cuts grass, most often called a lawn mower, in either a manual, an electric or a petrol model. Some larger ones are ride-on mowers that the user sits on. The word comes from the verb mow, and it rhymes with lower in the sense of moving down, with stress on the first syllable: MO-er. Typical collocations are push mower, riding mower and mower blade. Do not confuse it with a lawn trimmer, which is a hand tool for edges. In casual speech, people simply say lawnmower as one word.
x: He pushed the mower across the lawn every Saturday morning.
The blade of this mower needs sharpening before spring.
Our neighbors bought a ride-on mower for their huge garden.

paperback.n: A book with a flexible paper cover, cheaper than a hardback with a hard cover. It is a countable noun, but people also use it as a format label, as in available in paperback. Stress falls on the first syllable: PAY-per-bak. Authors often release a hardback first and a paperback a year later. Typical collocations are paperback edition, paperback novel and cheap paperback. It differs from an e-book, which is digital, and from a softcover, which is the same thing in a more formal catalog description. In casual speech, people say a paperback.
x: I bought a paperback to read on the long train journey.
The novel will come out in paperback next spring.
A paperback is lighter than a hardback, so it fits easily in a bag.

photocopier.n: A machine that makes copies of printed documents by using light and heat, commonly found in offices and libraries. It is a countable noun, and the stress falls on the first syllable: FO-to-kop-ee-er. People often shorten it to copier or copy machine, and in American English, the brand name Xerox is sometimes used generally. Typical collocations are use the photocopier, photocopier paper, jammed photocopier and photocopier toner. The verb is photocopy. A related device is a scanner, which makes a digital image instead of a paper copy.
x: Please use the photocopier near the reception desk for large jobs.
The photocopier ran out of toner just before the meeting.
A technician came to repair the photocopier on the second floor.

photographer.n: A person who takes photographs, either as a job or a hobby. Stress falls on the second syllable: fuh-TOG-ruh-fer, which surprises learners because the noun photograph stresses the first. Typical collocations are wedding photographer, press photographer, freelance photographer and amateur photographer. The related words are photography for the art and photograph for the picture. A press photographer works for news outlets, while a professional is paid. In casual speech, a person with a camera may be called a photographer even if just a keen amateur.
x: The wedding photographer stood on a chair to capture the whole group.
She works as a freelance photographer for travel magazines.
A press photographer waited outside the court for the verdict.

punctual.n: An adjective meaning arriving or acting exactly at the arranged time, neither late nor early. It describes people and also events, such as punctual trains. Stress falls on the first syllable: PUNK-choo-ul. The noun is punctuality, and the opposite is late or unpunctual. Typical patterns are be punctual for a meeting and punctual in paying bills. It sounds somewhat formal and is common in business and school contexts. Do not confuse it with on time as a simple phrase, which is more usual in daily talk. In some cultures, being punctual is highly valued.
x: Our teacher expects every student to be punctual for the first lesson.
The trains in this country are famously punctual.
He is always punctual in paying his rent, so the landlord trusts him.

purse.n: The meaning depends on region. In British English, it is a small bag or wallet for coins and cards, usually carried by a woman. In American English, it means a handbag. As a verb, to purse your lips means to tighten them, showing disapproval or thought. Stress is on the one syllable, rhyming with nurse. Typical collocations are leather purse, coin purse and purse strings, as in hold the purse strings, which means control the money. Do not confuse it with wallet, which is flatter and often used by men.
x: She took her keys and phone out of her purse at the door.
The teacher pursed her lips when she saw the messy desk.
The board holds the purse strings, so every budget needs their approval.

redecorate.n: A verb meaning to change how a room or building looks by painting, adding new wallpaper or replacing furnishings. It takes an object, as in redecorate the kitchen, and the noun is redecoration. Stress falls on the first syllable: ree-DEK-uh-rayt. The prefix re- suggests it was decorated before, so it is not used for a brand new room. It is a lighter job than renovate, which may involve structural work. Typical collocations are redecorate the hall, completely redecorate and planning to redecorate. In casual talk, people say do up.
x: We want to redecorate the living room before our guests arrive.
The owners plan to redecorate the whole hotel over the winter.
After they redecorated the nursery, it looked bright and cheerful.

relaxation.n: An uncountable noun for the state of being calm and free from tension, or for activities that help you reach it, such as music or a hot bath. A second sense means loosening of a rule, as in a relaxation of the law. Stress falls on the third syllable: ree-lak-SAY-shun. Typical collocations are relaxation techniques, a time for relaxation and muscle relaxation. The verb is relax, and relaxed is the adjective. A casual, everyday alternative is rest or downtime. It is neutral in register and common in wellness writing.
x: Yoga and slow breathing are popular methods of relaxation.
The new spa is designed purely for relaxation, with no phones allowed.
The government announced a relaxation of the travel rules.
